case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, in a False Claims Act qui tam suit in which the United States initially declined to intervene, the government may later move to dismiss the action and what standard governs the district court’s review of that dismissal request.
case_analysis.legal_provision: False Claims Act, 31 U.S.C. § 3730(c)(2)(A) (government authority to dismiss a qui tam action notwithstanding relator objections); related procedural background under § 3730(b) and (c).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The United States (supporting relator Polansky) argues that § 3730(c)(2)(A) gives the government broad discretion to dismiss a qui tam case even after declining intervention, and that courts should apply a deferential standard: once the government identifies a rational basis tied to legitimate governmental interests (e.g., litigation burdens, policy priorities, risk of adverse precedent), dismissal should generally be granted, with at most limited review for constitutional violations or egregious arbitrariness.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that the government’s dismissal power under § 3730(c)(2)(A) is not boundless and must be meaningfully constrained by judicial review; because the case proceeds in the name of the United States but is litigated by a private relator, a court should require the government to satisfy a more demanding standard (often framed as requiring intervention first and/or showing good cause and a valid, non-pretextual justification) and should protect defendants and relators from strategic, late-stage dismissal that undermines reliance interests and the FCA’s enforcement design.
key_precedents: Azar v. Allina Health Services, 139 S. Ct. 1804 (2019)
Allina Health Servs. v. Price, 863 F.3d 937 (D.C. Cir. 2017)
Select Specialty Hosp.-Denver, Inc. v. Azar, 391 F. Supp. 3d 53 (D.D.C. 2019)
Yale New Haven Hosp. v. Azar, 409 F. Supp. 3d 3 (D. Conn. 2019)
Wills v. Burwell, 306 F. Supp. 3d 684 (E.D. Pa. 2018)

John Roberts.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point remains the reliance/incentive concern: post-declination dismissal can appear to pull the rug out from under relators and Congress’s enforcement scheme. But as Justice Thomas and Justice Alito stress, § 3730(c)(2)(A) is categorical—authorizing dismissal “notwithstanding the objections” and conditioning it only on notice and a hearing—so importing an intervention-first limitation or a Sequoia Orange-style merits test would rewrite the statute and invite intrusive second-guessing of Executive enforcement judgments. Justice Sotomayor’s Rule 41(a)(2) analogy is a serious institutional caution, yet under a minimalist approach the “hearing” should function as a procedural check (and a backstop for unconstitutional or ultra vires action), not as a vehicle for courts to police “undue prejudice” or demand “good cause” where Congress did not. Consistent with Swift, a narrow holding recognizing dismissal authority even after declination, with highly deferential review limited to statutory compliance and legality/constitutionality, best preserves the statute’s text and institutional legitimacy while avoiding unnecessary Article II friction.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point remains reliance and incentive for relators after an initial declination, but that policy concern cannot overcome the unqualified text of § 3730(c)(2)(A), which authorizes the Government to “dismiss the action notwithstanding the objections” subject only to notice and a hearing. Justice Gorsuch’s observation that § 3730(c)(3) expressly addresses later intervention “for good cause” strengthens the conclusion that Congress anticipated ongoing Executive control after declination, rather than a forfeiture of dismissal authority. Justice Sotomayor is right that the hearing should not be purely ceremonial, but under an originalist/textualist approach we may police procedure and unconstitutional or ultra vires dismissals without importing a Rule 41(a)(2) or Sequoia Orange–style substantive prejudice/merits test that Congress did not enact. Chief Justice Roberts’s Swift-like, highly deferential review framework best fits the statutory design and avoids exacerbating Article II Take Care concerns inherent in private prosecution of federal claims.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—highlighted in Justice Sotomayor’s fairness concerns—is that post-declination dismissal can upset relators’ reliance and weaken Congress’s incentive scheme, but that policy intuition cannot overcome § 3730(c)(2)(A)’s categorical grant that the Government “may dismiss … notwithstanding the objections,” conditioned only on notice and a hearing. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas stress, the statute does not require prior intervention or a heightened merits showing, and importing a Rule 41(a)(2) undue-prejudice test would effectively convert the hearing requirement into a substantive veto Congress did not provide. Justice Gorsuch’s reference to § 3730(c)(3)’s “good cause” for later intervention reinforces that Congress anticipated continuing Executive control after declination, not a forfeiture of dismissal authority. Under a textualist approach attentive to practical consequences, Swift’s deferential framework—limited to ensuring procedural compliance and policing only unconstitutional or ultra vires dismissals—avoids unworkable satellite litigation and respects Executive enforcement discretion.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that post-declination dismissal can undercut Congress’s incentive structure for whistleblowers and may feel unfair after a relator has carried the case. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the text of § 3730(c)(2)(A) squarely authorizes dismissal “notwithstanding the objections” with notice and a hearing, and § 3730(c)(3) anticipates later intervention—so a forfeiture theory is hard to sustain. I do think Swift cannot be read to make the hearing meaningless; consistent with my fairness concerns, the district court should require the Government to articulate a legitimate, non-pretextual rationale and retain a modest ability to police unconstitutional or ultra vires dismissals, without sliding into Sequoia Orange-style merits litigation. On that understanding, I stay with Petitioner because it best fits the statutory scheme while still preserving a real, if deferential, safeguard for relators and program beneficiaries affected by fraud enforcement.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The strongest respondent point remains the reliance/incentives concern: that post-declination dismissal could encourage strategic Government reversals after the relator has invested heavily. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, § 3730(c)(2)(A)’s text contains no intervention-timing limitation and instead pairs a broad dismissal authorization (“may dismiss … notwithstanding the objections”) with procedural prerequisites (notice + hearing), while § 3730(c)(3)’s “good cause” later-intervention provision confirms Congress anticipated continued federal control after declination rather than forfeiture. Justice Sotomayor’s Rule 41(a)(2) analogy usefully underscores that the hearing cannot be a nullity, yet importing an “undue prejudice” or Sequoia Orange-style merits scrutiny would, on a pragmatic textualist reading, distort the statutory design and create unworkable satellite litigation that invites judicial second-guessing of Executive enforcement priorities. A workable middle ground is a meaningful hearing plus a deferential legality/rationality check (with room for constitutional or ultra vires challenges), which respects Congress’s procedural safeguard without rewriting it into a substantive veto.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument remains that post-declination dismissal would nullify the relator’s role and allow an end-run around § 3730(c)(3)’s “good cause” requirement for late intervention, but that reads a limitation into § 3730(c)(2)(A) that its unqualified text does not contain (“may dismiss … notwithstanding the objections”), apart from notice and a hearing. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, converting the hearing into Sequoia Orange-style merits review would effectively graft a substantive veto onto a provision Congress framed in procedural terms, and it would aggravate Article II concerns where the suit proceeds in the United States’ name. Justice Sotomayor’s Rule 41(a)(2) prejudice analogy usefully underscores that the hearing should be meaningful, but under a textualist/originalist approach it cannot become a free-ranging inquiry into the Government’s policy judgments; at most, courts may police constitutional violations or plainly ultra vires action. Justice Kagan’s workability point reinforces that a deferential legality-focused review best fits the statutory design without inviting satellite litigation over prosecutorial discretion.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains the reliance-and-incentives argument: post-declination dismissal could seem unfair to relators who invested heavily, and Justice Sotomayor is right that the § 3730(c)(2)(A) hearing cannot be a pure rubber stamp. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, the statutory text is unqualified—“may dismiss … notwithstanding the objections”—and § 3730(c)(3)’s “good cause” provision for later intervention reinforces that Congress expected continuing Executive control after declination, not forfeiture. Importing a Rule 41(a)(2) undue-prejudice or Sequoia Orange-style merits/pretext inquiry would, in practice, invite intrusive judicial supervision of enforcement priorities and satellite litigation, contrary to our institutional role and historical tradition of Executive control over federal litigation. The proper middle ground, consistent with Swift as framed by Roberts and Kagan, is deferential review that ensures procedural compliance and polices only constitutional or plainly ultra vires dismissals, which adequately answers fairness concerns without rewriting the statute.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest argument remains that post-declination dismissal should be unavailable (or conditioned on intervention/“good cause”) to preserve the relator’s incentive structure, but as Justice Gorsuch and Justice Thomas emphasize, § 3730(c)(2)(A) contains no such limitation and instead provides a specific safeguard—notice and an opportunity for a hearing—while § 3730(c)(3) separately addresses later intervention for “good cause,” indicating Congress knew how to impose that requirement when it wished. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan persuasively explain that importing a Sequoia Orange or Rule 41(a)(2)-style “undue prejudice” merits inquiry would rewrite the statute’s procedural hearing into a substantive veto over Executive enforcement decisions, heightening Article II concerns. I take Justice Sotomayor’s point that the hearing should not be purely ceremonial, but under a textualist approach its “bite” is satisfied by ensuring statutory compliance and policing constitutional or plainly ultra vires dismissals, not by judicial second-guessing of the Government’s litigation priorities. Vermont Agency’s partial-assignment framing further supports treating the United States as the real party in interest, making deferential review the best fit with the FCA’s text and structure.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point remains reliance and incentive: post-declination dismissal can feel like a bait-and-switch after a relator invests heavily, potentially chilling whistleblowers. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, § 3730(c)(2)(A) authorizes dismissal “notwithstanding the objections” and specifies the safeguard Congress chose—notice and a hearing—rather than a merits-based veto; grafting Sequoia Orange or a Rule 41(a)(2) undue-prejudice test would effectively rewrite that choice and predictably generate satellite litigation over executive enforcement priorities. I take Justice Sotomayor’s concern seriously, and I would insist the “hearing” be meaningful in the limited sense that the Government must articulate a lawful, rational reason and courts must police unconstitutional, discriminatory, or ultra vires dismissals, but that is consistent with Swift’s deferential framework rather than a heightened substantive standard. Section 3730(c)(3)’s contemplation of later intervention for “good cause,” as Justice Gorsuch notes, further undercuts any theory that an initial declination forfeits continuing federal control, so I remain with Petitioner.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 3730(c)(2)(A) gives the Government authority to “dismiss the action notwithstanding the objections of the [relator]” so long as the relator receives notice and an opportunity for a hearing, and nothing in the text makes that authority contingent on having intervened at the outset. To preserve institutional legitimacy and respect for executive enforcement discretion, a district court’s role should be limited to confirming statutory compliance and guarding against constitutional violations, not second-guessing policy judgments about burdens, priorities, or litigation risk. The more searching Sequoia Orange framework risks inviting intrusive merits review and inconsistency with the traditional presumption that enforcement decisions are generally committed to the Executive. A narrow holding recognizing the Government’s post-declination dismissal authority with highly deferential review best fits the statute’s structure and avoids unnecessary constitutional friction.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 31 U.S.C. § 3730(c)(2)(A) provides that "[t]he Government may dismiss the action notwithstanding the objections of the [relator]," and nothing in the provision limits that authority to cases where the United States intervened at the outset under § 3730(b)(4). Consistent with the Constitution’s original allocation of executive power, the Executive must retain sufficient control over litigation brought in the name of the United States; reading the FCA to bar post-declination dismissal would raise serious Article II Take Care concerns. Vermont Agency of Natural Resources v. United States ex rel. Stevens recognizes the relator as a “partial assignee” of the Government’s claim, which implies the Government remains the real party in interest and may terminate the delegated enforcement when it determines dismissal serves federal interests. Accordingly, district-court review should be limited and deferential, focused on the statutory hearing/notice requirement and guarding against constitutional violations or clear arbitrariness, rather than imposing a heightened “good cause” or intervention-first prerequisite absent from the statute’s text.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text of 31 U.S.C. § 3730(c)(2)(A) provides that “the Government may dismiss the action notwithstanding the objections of the [relator],” and nothing in that provision conditions dismissal on the Government’s having intervened at the outset or on a heightened, court-imposed “good cause” showing. A more searching merits review would improperly transfer core Executive control over litigation brought in the United States’ name to private relators and courts, with predictable practical costs (including litigation burdens, adverse-precedent risk, and interference with enforcement priorities). Consistent with Swift v. United States, 318 F.3d 250 (D.C. Cir. 2003), the district court should apply at most a deferential rationality/arbitrariness check and police only constitutional or plainly unlawful dismissals, rather than second-guessing the Government’s assessment of its interests. This reading best harmonizes § 3730(c)(2)(A) with the FCA’s broader structure in § 3730(b) and (c), which preserves substantial governmental control even when the relator initially conducts the action.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 3730(c)(2)(A) expressly authorizes the Government to “dismiss the action notwithstanding the objections” of the relator, and reading that authority to evaporate after an initial declination would undermine Congress’s design that the United States remains the real party in interest in FCA litigation. The better reading is that the Government may later intervene under § 3730(c)(3) upon a showing of “good cause” and then seek dismissal, with the district court applying a meaningful but deferential check—akin to Rule 41(a)(2)’s protection against undue prejudice—so that dismissals are not arbitrary or used to unfairly disadvantage relators who have carried the case. This approach preserves access to justice for whistleblowers and protects vulnerable beneficiaries of federal programs by keeping the FCA’s enforcement mechanism robust, while still respecting the Executive’s legitimate interests in managing litigation burdens and policy priorities. A more searching standard like Sequoia Orange risks inviting courts to second-guess core prosecutorial judgments, but some judicial backstop is warranted to ensure fairness and prevent pretextual dismissals.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 3730(c)(2)(A) states that “the Government may dismiss the action notwithstanding the objections” of the relator, subject only to notice and an opportunity for a hearing—text that naturally covers dismissal even when the Government initially declined to intervene under § 3730(b) and later intervenes under § 3730(c). Read as a coherent scheme, the statute preserves substantial Executive control over litigation brought in the United States’ name, while the hearing requirement supplies a procedural check that supports at least rationality-style review rather than a demanding merits inquiry. The D.C. Circuit’s approach in Swift v. United States—treating dismissal authority as broad once procedural requirements are met—best fits the textual command and promotes workability by avoiding prolonged collateral litigation over the Government’s enforcement priorities. A deferential standard (with room to police constitutional violations or truly arbitrary action) respects both the FCA’s purpose of encouraging relators and the Government’s superior institutional capacity to weigh burdens, policy priorities, and litigation risks.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 3730(c)(2)(A) says the Government “may dismiss the action notwithstanding the objections of the [relator]” so long as the relator receives notice and an opportunity for a hearing; nothing in that text limits dismissal to cases where the United States intervened at the outset, and § 3730(c)(3) expressly contemplates later intervention for “good cause,” underscoring continuing Executive control. Consistent with Vermont Agency of Natural Resources v. United States ex rel. Stevens, 529 U.S. 765 (2000), the relator proceeds by a partial assignment of the United States’ claim, and the Executive—responsible under Article II for litigation conducted in the Nation’s name—must retain authority to terminate that delegation. Judicial review should therefore be narrow and textual: confirm the statutory prerequisites (notice and hearing) and guard against constitutional or ultra vires action, but not superintend the Executive’s policy and resource judgments through heightened merits review. A more demanding, court-fashioned standard would add constraints Congress did not write and risk upsetting separation of powers by transferring core prosecutorial and litigation-disposition authority from the Executive to the Judiciary.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 3730(c)(2)(A) expressly authorizes the United States to “dismiss the action notwithstanding the objections” of the relator, and the statute’s structure in § 3730(c) contemplates that the Government may later assert control over a qui tam case even after initially declining to intervene. Consistent with history and tradition of Executive Branch control over litigation in the name of the United States, district-court review should be highly deferential and focused on basic rationality and legality rather than second-guessing enforcement priorities—an approach reflected in Swift v. United States’ emphasis on prosecutorial discretion and, even under Sequoia Orange, a rational relation to a valid governmental purpose. A more searching “good cause” or pretext inquiry would risk unworkable satellite litigation, undermine practical Executive enforcement judgments, and destabilize the FCA’s operation by discouraging later corrective intervention/dismissal decisions. On this record, the Government’s asserted interests (litigation burdens, policy priorities, and avoidance of adverse precedent) readily qualify as legitimate governmental interests under § 3730(c)(2)(A).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of § 3730(c)(2)(A) provides that "[t]he Government may dismiss the action notwithstanding the objections of the [relator]," and nothing in that provision conditions dismissal authority on the Government’s initial decision to intervene under § 3730(b)(4); reading in an irrevocable forfeiture would add a limitation the statute does not contain. Consistent with the FCA’s structure and Article II considerations, the relator litigates only as a partial assignee of the United States’ claim, Vermont Agency of Natural Resources v. United States ex rel. Stevens, 529 U.S. 765, 773 (2000), leaving the United States as the real party in interest with a continuing stake in controlling its litigation. Precedent also recognizes that the Government may intervene later upon a showing of good cause, § 3730(c)(3), which supports the conclusion that executive control mechanisms persist after an initial declination. Accordingly, district-court review of a § 3730(c)(2)(A) dismissal motion should be deferential, focused on whether the Government has articulated a rational basis tied to legitimate governmental interests, rather than a searching merits inquiry.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 3730(c)(2)(A) expressly authorizes the United States to “dismiss the action notwithstanding the objections” of the relator so long as the relator receives notice and “an opportunity for a hearing,” and that structure supports allowing dismissal even after an initial declination to intervene under § 3730(b) and (c). Consistent with Sequoia Orange, the district court’s role should be limited to ensuring procedural fairness and guarding against unconstitutional or egregiously arbitrary action, not second-guessing executive enforcement judgments; requiring a heightened merits showing or effectively conditioning dismissal on earlier intervention would add a constraint Congress did not write. This deferential, rational-relation review also better accounts for practical consequences, including litigation burdens, resource allocation, and the government’s interest in avoiding adverse precedent that can distort broader FCA enforcement. A meaningful hearing requirement remains important to protect the relator’s participation and to ensure the government’s stated reasons are not pretext for impermissible discrimination or other constitutional violations.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, in an FCA qui tam action where the United States initially declined to intervene, the government may later move to dismiss the suit and what standard governs the district court’s review of that dismissal request.
case_analysis.legal_provision: False Claims Act, 31 U.S.C. § 3730(c)(2)(A) (government authority to dismiss a qui tam action notwithstanding the relator’s objections, after notice and an opportunity for a hearing).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The United States argues that § 3730(c)(2)(A) gives the Executive Branch broad, largely discretionary power to dismiss a qui tam action even after declining intervention; once it provides notice and a hearing opportunity, dismissal should be granted absent extraordinary circumstances (at most limited judicial review, often framed as rational-relation or akin to prosecutorial discretion). The government also contends it may seek dismissal without first formally intervening (or may intervene for the limited purpose of dismissal), because the statute makes the United States the real party in interest and preserves executive control over litigation brought in its name.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (defendants) generally support a rule enabling government-initiated dismissal and seek a clear, deferential standard that avoids protracted merits litigation when the United States concludes the case is not in its interests. They emphasize that allowing relators to force continuation despite government opposition undermines executive enforcement prerogatives and imposes significant litigation and settlement pressure on defendants, and they oppose heightened judicial scrutiny that would invite mini-trials over DOJ’s reasons.
key_precedents: Azar v. Allina Health Services, 139 S. Ct. 1804 (2019)
Allina Health Services v. Price, 863 F.3d 937 (D.C. Cir. 2017)
Select Specialty Hosp.-Denver, Inc. v. Azar, 391 F. Supp. 3d 53 (D.D.C. 2019)
Yale New Haven Hosp. v. Azar, 409 F. Supp. 3d 3 (D. Conn. 2019)
Wills v. Burwell, 306 F. Supp. 3d 684 (E.D. Pa. 2018)

John Roberts.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument remains that the “opportunity for a hearing” becomes meaningless if courts cannot meaningfully review a dismissal, but—as Justice Kagan notes—the hearing can do real work as a procedural safeguard (notice and an opportunity to contest illegality, bad faith, or ultra vires action) without inviting a merits inquiry into DOJ’s enforcement judgments. Justice Sotomayor’s modest Sequoia Orange–style rational-relation test is appealing as a policy matter, yet under a minimalist approach it risks hardening into structured, intrusive review that Congress did not clearly authorize and that would exacerbate Article II tensions. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Polansky reinforces the narrow, text-based resolution: later intervention (including for dismissal) is permissible, and the district court’s role should be highly deferential—closer to Rule 41(a)—rather than a multi-factor scrutiny that would turn hearings into mini-trials. A restrained holding can preserve the hearing requirement’s procedural bite while avoiding judicial second-guessing and protecting institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that the “opportunity for a hearing” would be meaningless if courts could not examine anything; but the text of § 3730(c)(2)(A) answers that by authorizing dismissal “notwithstanding the objections,” which presupposes that objections may be aired yet not converted into a judicial veto over Executive enforcement decisions. Justice Sotomayor’s proposed Sequoia Orange-style rational-relation test still adds a substantive limitation Congress did not write, and—under an originalist separation-of-powers understanding—invites Article II intrusion by letting courts supervise prosecutorial discretion in a suit brought in the United States’ name. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Polansky reinforces that the Government may intervene after declination to move to dismiss, and any judicial role should be confined to policing illegality (e.g., constitutional defects, ultra vires action, fraud on the court), not evaluating the wisdom of dismissal. I therefore maintain my vote for petitioner and would reject heightened scrutiny as inconsistent with the statute’s ordinary meaning and structure.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that § 3730(c)(2)(A)’s “opportunity for a hearing” must do some work, but as the Chief Justice explains, that work is procedural—notice and a chance to be heard—rather than a judicial license to second-guess the Executive’s enforcement judgment. Justice Sotomayor’s proposed Sequoia Orange-style rational-relation check has intuitive appeal as a fairness measure, yet it still invites intrusive, quasi-merits review untethered to the statute’s text, which says the Government “may dismiss … notwithstanding” relator objections once notice and a hearing occur. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Polansky further undercuts any implied early-intervention condition by confirming later intervention is contemplated and that dismissal review should resemble Rule 41(a)-type deference. On a textualist reading attentive to practical consequences and Article II, courts should police only for illegality, constitutional defect, or clear irrationality—not impose a structured multi-factor scrutiny that effectively empowers relators to keep litigation going in the United States’ name.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point remains that an “opportunity for a hearing” becomes largely performative if courts apply Swift-like near-total deference, inviting arbitrary or captured dismissals that chill relators and can harm the public fisc. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett that nothing in § 3730(c)(2)(A) imposes an early-intervention forfeiture rule, and Barrett’s reliance on Polansky appropriately confirms the Government may later intervene for purposes of dismissal. But Roberts’s and Justice Thomas’s framing of the hearing as purely procedural goes too far under my pragmatic approach: the statute’s hearing requirement must have some substantive bite—at least requiring DOJ to state a concrete, reviewable reason and permitting a modest rational-relation/legality check—without turning the proceeding into a merits trial or second-guessing core enforcement priorities. That middle ground addresses Article II concerns while ensuring fairness and meaningful access to justice for whistleblowers who vindicate vulnerable interests.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point remains that an “opportunity for a hearing” should entail some meaningful judicial check, but the text—“the Government may dismiss… notwithstanding the objections”—reads most naturally as preserving Executive control while guaranteeing process rather than merits review. Justice Sotomayor is right that a hearing cannot be a pure formality; I would therefore allow a limited rationality/legality screen (no unconstitutional, ultra vires, or bad-faith/sham dismissals) without importing Sequoia Orange’s more structured scrutiny that risks unworkable, intrusive second-guessing of enforcement choices. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Polansky strengthens the coherence of allowing post-declination intervention for dismissal and undercuts any implied early-intervention forfeiture rule that the statute’s text does not supply. Chief Justice Roberts’s Rule 41(a)-like framing is consistent with this middle-ground approach: the relator gets to be heard, but the court does not sit as a super-prosecutor over litigation brought in the United States’ name.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that the “opportunity for a hearing” must have some function, but the text still provides the Government “may dismiss … notwithstanding the objections,” which strongly signals a procedural right to be heard rather than a judicial power to second-guess Executive enforcement priorities. Justice Sotomayor’s suggestion of a Sequoia Orange–style rational-relation inquiry is attractive as a policy matter, yet—absent clearer statutory direction—it risks importing a substantive limitation that aggravates Article II “Take Care” concerns by inviting courts to police prosecutorial judgments. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Polansky reinforces that the FCA contemplates later intervention (including for dismissal) and supports aligning the district court’s role with Rule 41(a)’s traditionally deferential framework, leaving room only for narrow review for illegality, fraud on the court, or constitutional defect. On an originalist/textualist account, we should not transform a guaranteed hearing into an implied judicial veto over the Executive’s decision to end litigation brought in the United States’ name.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The strongest respondent point remains that § 3730(c)(2)(A)’s “opportunity for a hearing” would be hollow if courts apply near-total deference, but that argument still overreads “hearing” as a substantive constraint rather than a procedural guarantee; the text says the Government “may dismiss,” which strongly signals executive primacy once notice and an opportunity to be heard are provided. Chief Justice Roberts’s institutional concern is persuasive to me: importing Sequoia Orange-style structured scrutiny would invite intrusive discovery and mini-trials into DOJ’s motivations, undermining both workability and the Court’s legitimacy in second-guessing core enforcement judgments. At the same time, Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson helpfully identify a middle ground—limited policing for illegality, constitutional defect, or wholly irrational/sham dismissals—so the hearing is not a nullity without turning it into merits review. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Polansky reinforces that later intervention (even for dismissal) is contemplated by the statute, eliminating any plausible textual basis for an early-intervention forfeiture rule.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The strongest respondent point—pressed by Justice Sotomayor—is that an “opportunity for a hearing” must entail meaningful judicial scrutiny, but the text of § 3730(c)(2)(A) pairs that process guarantee with an affirmative grant that the Government “may dismiss … notwithstanding the objections,” which is difficult to square with a judicial veto or a Sequoia Orange–style merits inquiry. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan note, importing an early-intervention forfeiture rule finds no footing in the statute and clashes with § 3730(c)(3)’s express contemplation of later intervention for “good cause,” a point reinforced by Polansky’s recognition that post-declination intervention can support dismissal. Justice Gorsuch’s Article II concerns sharpen why the hearing is best understood as a procedural safeguard (notice and an opportunity to contest illegality, fraud, or ultra vires action) rather than a license for courts to second-guess enforcement priorities. I therefore maintain that the Government may intervene later to move to dismiss and that review should remain narrow and deferential, akin to Rule 41(a), with room only for policing constitutional or legal defects.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that near-plenary dismissal power after declination risks making the relator’s statutory role—and the “opportunity for a hearing”—illusory and vulnerable to captured or politically motivated decisions. But I agree with Justice Sotomayor that the hearing must have procedural bite: the Government should be required to give a concrete, reviewable explanation and be subject to a modest rationality/legality check that screens out arbitrariness, discrimination, or ultra vires action, without turning § 3730(c)(2)(A) into merits litigation over enforcement priorities. At the same time, Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan persuasively explain why an early-intervention forfeiture rule is textually unsupported and pragmatically destabilizing, and Justice Barrett’s reliance on Polansky reinforces that later intervention for dismissal coheres with the statutory structure. On my progressive-pragmatist view, the middle path best respects the Executive’s Article II interests while ensuring the FCA’s hearing requirement functions as a meaningful fairness safeguard rather than a formality.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 3730(c)(2)(A) authorizes the United States to “dismiss the action” so long as the relator receives notice and an opportunity for a hearing, and nothing in that text limits dismissal to cases where the Government intervened at the outset. Reading an early-intervention ultimatum into the statute would create unnecessary constitutional tension with the Executive’s traditional control over litigation brought in the United States’ name and would invite intrusive judicial second-guessing that undermines institutional legitimacy. Consistent with the Court’s understanding that the Government “retains the right at any time to dismiss the action entirely,” the Government may seek dismissal after initially declining intervention, with district-court review proceeding on narrow, deferential grounds (e.g., under Rule 41(a) and ordinary abuse-of-discretion principles) rather than heightened scrutiny. A restrained approach respects precedent, keeps the decision narrow, and avoids turning § 3730(c)(2)(A) hearings into merits trials over DOJ’s enforcement judgments.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 3730(c)(2)(A) provides that “the Government may dismiss the action notwithstanding the objections of the [relator]” after notice and an opportunity for a hearing; the text contains no requirement that the United States first intervene or satisfy a heightened, multi-factor judicial inquiry. Reading additional constraints into that grant would contradict the statute’s ordinary meaning and would aggravate serious Article II concerns by allowing a private relator to force continuation of litigation brought in the United States’ name despite the Executive’s contrary judgment. A deferential standard is therefore compelled, akin to prosecutorial discretion, with the hearing serving primarily to ensure notice and to allow the relator to be heard, not to authorize courts to second-guess Executive policy judgments. To the extent any precedent suggests broader judicial supervision, it should yield to the statutory text and the separation-of-powers principles implicated by qui tam enforcement.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 3730(c)(2)(A) states that “the Government may dismiss the action notwithstanding the objections of the [relator]” so long as the relator receives notice and an opportunity for a hearing, and nothing in the text conditions that authority on having intervened at the outset. Reading the statute to strip the Executive of dismissal authority after an initial declination would create serious Article II and practical-consequences problems by allowing private relators to commandeer litigation brought in the United States’ name, contrary to the premise that the suit vindicates a governmental injury and functions as a partial assignment of the Government’s claim. Vermont Agency of Natural Resources v. United States ex rel. Stevens recognizes both the partial-assignment character of qui tam and the need for mechanisms preserving executive control, and United States ex rel. Eisenstein confirms the United States remains the real party in interest even when it declines to intervene. Given that structure, district-court review of a dismissal motion should be highly deferential (at most ensuring notice/hearing and a facially rational basis), not an intrusive merits inquiry.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 3730(c)(2)(A) expressly authorizes the United States to “dismiss the action notwithstanding the objections” of the relator after notice and an opportunity for a hearing, and that authority should not evaporate merely because the Government initially declined to intervene. But the statutory hearing requirement would be largely meaningless if dismissal were treated as essentially unreviewable prosecutorial discretion; a modest, deferential check like Sequoia Orange’s “valid governmental purpose” and “rational relation” framework best respects both the text and the relator’s role while preventing arbitrary dismissals that could undermine accountability and access to justice. That standard preserves broad Executive control over litigation brought in the Government’s name, yet ensures the Government gives a concrete, reviewable explanation—especially important where the real-world impact falls on whistleblowers and the public fisc. Accordingly, I would allow later dismissal, without demanding full intervention, but require at least Sequoia Orange–style rational-basis review rather than Swift’s near-total deference.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 3730(c)(2)(A) provides that “the Government may dismiss the action notwithstanding the objections of the [relator]” so long as the relator receives notice and an opportunity for a hearing, and nothing in that text limits dismissal to cases where the United States intervened at the outset; reading such a limitation in would undermine the statutory scheme’s coherence and the Government’s role as the real party in interest. The hearing requirement is best understood as ensuring a procedurally fair chance for the relator to be heard, not as inviting searching merits-like review of Executive enforcement judgments, which would be unworkable and in tension with traditional prosecutorial discretion. Consistent with Swift v. United States, district courts should apply at most a highly deferential rationality check (or similarly limited review) to ensure the dismissal is not fraudulent, unconstitutional, or ultra vires, while otherwise respecting Executive control over litigation brought in the United States’ name. That approach preserves statutory purpose—encouraging relators to surface fraud—without allowing relators to force continued litigation the Government has concluded disserves federal interests.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 3730(c)(2)(A) states that "[t]he Government may dismiss the action" over the relator’s objection so long as the relator receives notice and an opportunity for a hearing; that plain text presupposes executive control over litigation brought in the United States’ name and leaves little room for a court to second-guess the Executive’s judgment. Reading the provision to require searching judicial scrutiny would invert the statute’s allocation of authority and raise serious separation-of-powers concerns by allowing a private relator to effectively compel continuation of federal enforcement litigation. The best reading is that the Government may seek dismissal even after an initial declination so long as it later intervenes (at least for purposes of dismissal), and the district court’s review is highly deferential—akin to ensuring a rational basis and absence of fraud or constitutional violation rather than a merits inquiry. This approach aligns with the statute’s structure preserving the Government as real party in interest and with the deferential frameworks adopted by lower courts under § 3730(c)(2)(A).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 3730(c)(2)(A) expressly authorizes the United States to “dismiss the action” notwithstanding the relator’s objections after notice and an opportunity for a hearing, and the FCA’s structure contemplates that the Government may later participate upon a showing of “good cause,” § 3730(c)(3), which in turn makes the dismissal mechanism workable even after an initial declination. Requiring the Executive to remain bound by an initial non-intervention decision would be difficult to square with the United States as the real party in interest and with traditional executive control over litigation conducted in the Government’s name. The district court’s review should be highly deferential—akin to rational-basis review reflected in Sequoia Orange—because a more searching inquiry would invite protracted mini-trials over DOJ’s reasons and undermine the practical workability of the statute’s dismissal provision. That approach respects the statutory text, preserves historical executive enforcement prerogatives, and avoids destabilizing qui tam practice through expansive judicial second-guessing.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 3730(c)(2)(A) provides that “the Government may dismiss the action notwithstanding the objections of the [relator]” so long as the relator receives notice and “an opportunity for a hearing,” and that text does not condition dismissal authority on the Government’s having intervened at the outset. Reading the statute in context, the FCA repeatedly treats the suit as one brought in the United States’ name and interests, so preserving Executive control over whether the action continues accords with the provision’s ordinary meaning and avoids serious Article II “Take Care” concerns. Precedent confirms this understanding: in United States ex rel. Polansky v. Executive Health Resources, Inc., 599 U.S. 419 (2023), the Court held the Government may move to dismiss after initially declining, provided it intervenes (including for the limited purpose of dismissal), and district courts should apply a deferential standard akin to Rule 41(a), granting dismissal absent a showing that it is arbitrary, capricious, or illegal. That approach respects the statutory hearing requirement while maintaining methodological consistency with the Executive’s traditional prosecutorial discretion in controlling litigation brought on its behalf.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 3730(c)(2)(A) expressly authorizes the United States to “dismiss the action notwithstanding the objections of the [relator]” so long as the relator receives notice and an opportunity for a hearing, and nothing in that text plausibly limits dismissal authority to cases where the Government intervened at the outset. Consistent with widespread circuit practice, the Government may intervene later (including for the limited purpose of seeking dismissal) and then move to dismiss, with district-court review focused on procedural fairness and a modest check against arbitrary action rather than a merits mini-trial. A deferential standard best aligns with the FCA’s structure—where the United States remains the real party in interest—and avoids the practical consequence of forcing continued litigation in the Government’s name when DOJ concludes the suit disserves federal enforcement priorities. The hearing requirement still matters: courts should ensure the relator can be heard and that the Government articulates a rational basis, but not second-guess enforcement judgments absent extraordinary circumstances.
